terms.meaning: Confidentiality, integrity, availability: the three goals in the US legal definition of infosec (44 U.S.C. 3552).
Preserving authorized restrictions on access and disclosure, incl. personal privacy and proprietary information.
Guarding against improper modification or destruction; includes nonrepudiation and authenticity.
Ensuring timely and reliable access to and use of information.
Authentication, authorization, accounting: who you are, what you may do, and a record of what you did.
Layering independent controls so that the failure of any single one does not lead to compromise.

spec.as: Layer the controls so no single failure opens the whole door.

terms.meaning: Grant only the access a task needs; a 1975 design principle and control AC-6 in NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.
Base access on explicit permission, not exclusion: the default answer is deny. A 1975 design principle.
terms.reference: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (1975)

spec.as: When in doubt, deny: access needs explicit permission.

terms.meaning: Check every access to every object for authority, not just the first one. A 1975 design principle.
terms.reference: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (1975)

spec.as: Check every access to every object, every single time.

terms.meaning: The design should not be secret; security rests on protected keys, not on attackers' ignorance. A 1975 design principle.
terms.reference: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (1975)

spec.as: The design is public; only the keys stay secret.

terms.meaning: Protection must be easy to use so people apply it routinely and correctly. A 1975 design principle.
terms.reference: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (1975)

terms.meaning: Relying on secrecy of design or implementation as the main defense; corrected by the open design principle.
NIST model (Aug 2020): no implicit trust from network location; every access is authenticated and authorized.
Perimeter model (trusted inside, hostile outside) that zero trust drops: location grants no trust (SP 800-207).
Pre-approved emergency access account or procedure, used only when normal access fails, and always audited.
Visible measures that make people feel safer without materially reducing risk.
Fear, uncertainty and doubt: selling security by scaring buyers instead of informing them.
Jargon for the human user, one layer above the seven of the OSI model; blamed for many incidents.
A vulnerability unknown to the vendor or with no fix yet: defenders have had zero days to respond.
Hacker and gamer slang for 'owned': compromised or thoroughly defeated.
Unskilled attacker who runs tools written by others without understanding them.
Leetspeak for 'elite': letters swapped for lookalike digits (1 for l, 3 for E, 7 for T).

terms.text: White hat · Grey hat · Black hat
terms.meaning: Hacker ethics spectrum: authorized defender, unauthorized but not malicious, and malicious attacker.

terms.text: Red team · Blue team · Purple team
terms.meaning: Adversary emulation, defense, and both working together to improve detection and response.
The Jargon File reserves 'cracker' (coined ca. 1985) for one who breaks security; a hacker is an enthusiast.
Culture of sharing, openness, decentralization and hands-on curiosity from early computing labs.
Cult of the Dead Cow: hacker group and ezine founded June 1984 in Lubbock, Texas; a member coined 'hacktivism' (1996).
Hacker lexicon begun in 1975; last version 4.4.7 dated Dec 29, 2003. In print: The New Hacker's Dictionary.
Hacker ezine first published Nov 17, 1985; issue #72 (Aug 19, 2025) is its 40th-anniversary edition.
The 'Hacker Manifesto', written Jan 8, 1986; Phrack Volume One, Issue 7 (Sept 25, 1986), Phile 3 of 10.
Hacker magazine launched January 1984, named after the 2600 Hz long-distance trunk tone.
In-band trunk tone whose 1960s discovery gave access to 'operator mode'; the emblem of phone phreaking.
Zine of proof-of-concept hacking; issue 0x00 is dated Aug 5, 2013. Known for polyglot PDF issues.
'Data slingshot': the Chaos Computer Club's magazine, published since 1984.
Chaos Computer Club, hacker association founded Sept 12, 1981 in West Berlin.
39th Chaos Communication Congress, Dec 27–30, 2025, Congress Center Hamburg. First Congress: 1984.
The 34th DEF CON, Aug 6–9, 2026, Las Vegas Convention Center West Hall. The first was held June 9–11, 1993.
Nickname for the August week in Las Vegas that bundles Black Hat, BSides Las Vegas and DEF CON.
DEF CON's highest honor, won in select contests such as its CTF; grants free entry for life.
Display of partly masked credentials seen in cleartext on the con network; at DEF CON since 2002.
Community-run security conferences, born in 2009 from talks Black Hat USA's CFP had no room for.
Renamed in early 2025; the added C stands for community. Flagship event held yearly in San Francisco.
Use what is said, but reveal neither the identity nor the affiliation of speakers or participants. Since 1927.
TLP 2.0 (Aug 2022) renamed WHITE to CLEAR: recipients can spread it to the world, no limit on disclosure.
TLP 2.0 label that restricts sharing to the recipient's organization only.
TLP 2.0 label: for the eyes and ears of individual recipients only, no further disclosure.
TLP 2.0 label: limited disclosure, only on a need-to-know basis within the recipient's organization and its clients.
TLP 2.0 label: limited disclosure, recipients can spread it within their community.
CERT Coordination Center, created Nov 1988 at Carnegie Mellon's SEI in response to the Internet worm.
Exchanging cyber threat information with partners under agreed handling rules, as guided by NIST SP 800-150 (Oct 2016).
Information Sharing and Analysis Center: a community, often of one sector, whose members share cyber threat information.
Microsoft's monthly security release on the second Tuesday, formalized Oct 2003; also called Update Tuesday.
File telling researchers how to report vulnerabilities (Apr 2022); Contact and Expires fields are required.
Finders and vendors coordinate a fix before publication; the neutral name for what was 'responsible disclosure'.
Replacements for 'whitelist' and 'blacklist'; OWASP cheat sheets use them ('Allowlist vs Denylist').
Internet Security Glossary, Version 2 (Aug 2007); obsoletes RFC 2828.
Site Security Handbook (FYI 8, Sept 1997); obsoletes RFC 1244.
The Security Flag in the IPv4 Header: April 1, 2003 joke RFC defining the 'evil bit'.
Classic geek joke: the loopback address is home.
TCSEC, 1985 edition; centerpiece of the Rainbow Series, canceled Oct 24, 2002. Succeeded by Common Criteria.
Orange Book evaluation classes, from minimal protection (D) to verified design (A1).
Evaluation standard (ISO/IEC 15408, CC:2022) with seven assurance levels, EAL1 to EAL7.

terms.text: No read up · No write down
terms.meaning: Classic multilevel confidentiality rules: the simple security property and the *-property.

mat.as: no read up · no write down

terms.text: No read down · No write up
terms.meaning: Mirror-image rules of classic multilevel integrity models; the lookalike twin of the confidentiality rules.

mat.as: no read down · no write up

terms.meaning: Cybersecurity Framework, Feb 26, 2024: 6 Functions, 22 Categories, 106 Subcategories.

terms.text: GV · ID · PR · DE · RS · RC
terms.meaning: The six CSF 2.0 Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Govern is new in 2.0.
CSF 1.1 access control Category withdrawn and moved to PR.AA (Identity Mgmt, Authentication, Access Control).
1.1 (Apr 2018) was 'Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity'; 2.0 is for all organizations.
ISMS requirements, Oct 2022; Annex A has 93 controls. All 2013-edition certificates expired Oct 31, 2025.
Climate action changes (Feb 2024): clause 4.1 now asks whether climate change is a relevant issue for the ISMS.
Control guidance: 93 controls in 4 themes: organizational 37, people 8, physical 14, technological 34.
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A themes: organizational, people, physical and technological controls.
Annex A went from 114 controls in 14 clauses (2013) to 93 controls in 4 themes (2022), 11 of them new.
ISO/IEC 27001 clause 6.1.3 d): lists necessary controls, why each is included or excluded, and its status.
Sixth edition (July 3, 2026): title now ends 'Overview', no longer 'Overview and vocabulary'; replaces 27000:2018.
A system's impact level is the highest of its confidentiality, integrity and availability impact values.
NIST catalog of security and privacy controls in 20 families; Rev. 5 was published in Sept 2020.

terms.text: AC AT AU CA CM CP IA IR MA MP
terms.meaning: First ten SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control family IDs, Access Control through Media Protection.

terms.text: PE PL PM PS PT RA SA SC SI SR
terms.meaning: Last ten family IDs, Physical and Environmental Protection through Supply Chain Risk Management.
Lookalikes: 800-53 is the control catalog; 800-63-4 (July 2025) is the Digital Identity Guidelines.
18 Controls; the 56 Safeguards of IG1 define essential cyber hygiene. v8.1 added a Govern function.
The certification body dropped the parentheses and superscript on Aug 17, 2023.
ISC2 certification in 8 domains, from Security and Risk Management to Software Development Security.
Codename in the 1992 film Sneakers; an anagram of 'too many secrets'.
SP 800-53A finding: potential anomalies in the control, or too little information to decide. The other is satisfied (S).
RMF decision (SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Task R-4): the authorizing official accepts the risk and the system may operate.
Orange Book division for systems that were evaluated but failed to meet a higher class. It was TCSEC's failing grade.
The Have I Been Pwned result when a searched email address appears in the data breaches it has loaded.
The Have I Been Pwned result when a searched email address is in none of the data breaches it has loaded.
The belief Forrester founded zero trust on in 2009: trust itself is the weakness, so never trust and always verify.
Microsoft's first Zero Trust principle: authenticate and authorize every request using all available signals.
A 1975 design principle: a mechanism that needs two keys to unlock is more robust and flexible than one key.
A tenet of the Hacker Ethic as written down in Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution (1984).
Law #10 of Microsoft's Ten Immutable Laws of Security: no product delivers security by itself.
Trust granted because of network position, not because anything was proven: the gap zero trust removes.
CSF 1.1 Category ID.BE (Business Environment) was withdrawn and moved into GV.OC.
CSF 1.1 Category ID.RM (Risk Management Strategy) was withdrawn and moved into GV.RM.
CSF 1.1 Category RS.RP (Response Planning) was withdrawn and moved into RS.MA.
Latin x and Cyrillic ha look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin y and Cyrillic u look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin a and Cyrillic a look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin e and Cyrillic ie look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin o and Cyrillic o look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Known-answer test: the 68-byte antivirus test file, harmless text every scanner flags; MD5 first 64 bits shown.
Known-answer test: the SHA-256 of the 68-byte EICAR test file, first 96 bits shown.
Known-answer test: 6-digit HOTP for counter 1 with the RFC 4226 Appendix D key.
Known-answer test: 8-digit TOTP with HMAC-SHA-1, the RFC 6238 Appendix B key and Unix time 59.
CSF 2.0 Detect category, called Anomalies and Events in CSF 1.1; 2.0 dropped DE.DP Detection Processes.
FIRST Traffic Light Protocol label for information that may be shared publicly; replaced TLP:WHITE.
Deprecated TLP 1.0 label; replaced by TLP:CLEAR when TLP 2.0 took effect in August 2022.
Analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident and the root cause of the incident.
Incident data and metadata are collected, and their integrity and provenance are preserved.
CSF 1.1 "Forensics are performed". CSF 2.0 rescoped it into RS.AN-03 (analysis) and RS.AN-06 (records).
Terminology shift: 'allowlist' and 'denylist' replace the older terms in docs and tools.
Ken Thompson's 1984 Turing Award lecture: a trojaned compiler can plant a backdoor no source-level review finds.
Multilevel confidentiality model by David Bell and Leonard LaPadula, set out in MITRE reports of the 1970s.
Integrity model by Kenneth Biba, the dual of Bell–LaPadula: it guards data against improper modification.
Security industry conference first held in Las Vegas in 1997, followed days later by DEF CON.
Access to specific information only for those whose official duties require it, on top of any clearance.

spec.as: Clearance opens the door; need to know opens the file.

terms.meaning: AICPA examination report on a service organization's controls against the five Trust Services Criteria.
Rewards paid to outside researchers who report security flaws in an organization's software or services.
MSRC reframed 'Responsible Disclosure' as Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure in July 2010; CERT/CC also advocates CVD.
